examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Critical Points of Trigonometric Functions
examples.problem: Consider the function $f(x) = \sqrt 3\sin{2x} - \cos{2x}.$ Find critical points of $f(x)$ for $x \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$
examples.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x} & =-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡2x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{n\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \lt x \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \lt x \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ are 

$$
x =-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \qquad x =  \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x =-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

- Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in \left(-\dfrac\pi2, \dfrac\pi2\right).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in \left(-\dfrac\pi2, \dfrac\pi2\right)$ are

$$
x_1 =-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \qquad x_2 =  \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

feedback.problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+3}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+3}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+3)-(x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}+3)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+3)-(x+1)\cdot (2x)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3-2{x}^{2}-2x}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3-2x-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3-2x-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} & =0 \\ 3-2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-3 & =0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =-3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-3$ and $x=1.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-3$ and $x=1.$
